Overview

What this trek actually is

The Annapurna Sanctuary is a bowl. You walk up a river valley that narrows for three days until the walls close in on both sides, and then it opens into a flat glacial basin with ten mountains standing around it. That basin is Annapurna Base Camp, 4,130 m. There is no pass to cross and no summit to reach. You walk in, you sleep there, you walk out. This is the seven day version, run from our own office in Lakeside with a licensed female guide and a group of no more than eight.

The route starts with a 3 hour jeep to Jhinu Danda. From there it is three days up through Chhomrong, Sinuwa, Deurali and Machhapuchhre Base Camp, then three days back down through Bamboo, Jhinu Danda and Ghandruk. You cross six suspension bridges. Breakfast is at first light, you are walking by seven, and most days are four to seven hours with a proper lunch stop at a teahouse on the way. Most afternoons you are in by two or three, which leaves time to dry your things, drink tea and watch the cloud come up the valley. There is no technical ground anywhere on this route. It is stone steps, forest path and, above Deurali, an open valley floor. You sleep in teahouses the whole way, in Gurung villages rather than tents, with a bed and a hot meal every night. The rooms are plain: two beds, a blanket and a shared bathroom once you are above Chhomrong. The difficulty is repetition and altitude, not skill. Anyone who walks regularly and can manage a long day on their feet can do this.

The two things that make it hard

The first is the ground on day one and day five. Below Chhomrong you walk down about 3,300 stone steps and then straight back up the other side of the river, and on the way home you do the same in reverse. Everybody talks about those steps afterwards. It is not dangerous, it is relentless, and it lands on the first day on purpose so the rest of the week gets easier rather than harder.

The second is the last night up. Base camp is 4,130 m, high enough that some people sleep badly and wake with a headache. That is why the day before it is kept short, and why we go up and come straight back down rather than lingering. Both of these are covered honestly further down this page, in the difficulty and safety sections.

Why we start in Pokhara and not Kathmandu

Most companies selling this trek are based in Kathmandu, and their versions run 11 to 14 days because four of those days are travel: two hotel nights in Kathmandu, the road to Pokhara and the road back. Per walking day their price is only a little above ours once you compare the same group size. The real difference is the days. If you are already in Pokhara, or flying into Pokhara, you do not need them. If you want the Kathmandu sightseeing, we will book it separately so you can see exactly what it costs and decide for yourself.

Itinerary

Day by day

Day 1 is open. The rest expand. Nothing collapses again on its own.

Download itinerary as PDF →
Day 1 · Pokhara to Jhinu Danda by jeep, then trek to Sinuwa 5 to 6 hours walking · 12 km · +970 m / -390 m · Sleep at 2,360 m

A 3 hour jeep from our office in Lakeside gets you to Jhinu Danda by mid-morning. Then the hard part of the week arrives on day one, on purpose, so the rest of the trek gets easier rather than harder. You climb to Chhomrong at 2,170 m, which takes about two hours. Chhomrong is where you get your last bakery, your last reliable hot shower and your last shop.

After lunch the trail drops down roughly 3,300 stone steps to the Chhomrong Khola, crosses a suspension bridge, and climbs straight back up the other side to Sinuwa. There is no way around it and no vehicle that can take you. Everybody finds it hard and nobody has failed to finish it. Machhapuchhre is directly ahead of you for most of the afternoon.

BLD Sleep: Sinuwa Guest House or similar, teahouse, twin share

Day 2 · Sinuwa to Deurali 6 hours walking · 13 km · +880 m / -60 m · Sleep at 3,180 m

The valley narrows today and the rhododendron forest closes over the trail. You drop through Bamboo at 2,310 m, then climb steadily through Dovan to Himalaya and on to Deurali. The walls on both sides get higher all day and the sky above you gets narrower.

This is the first night above 3,000 m. Your guide starts checking your oxygen saturation this evening and writes it down. Drink more than you feel like drinking.

BLD Sleep: Deurali, teahouse, twin share

Day 3 · Deurali to Annapurna Base Camp, by way of Machhapuchhre Base Camp 5 hours walking · 9 km · +950 m · Sleep at 4,130 m

The biggest climbing day, and the shortest in distance, which tells you what the ground is doing. You walk out of the trees and into the sanctuary. Machhapuchhre Base Camp at 3,700 m is where you stop for lunch and where most people first notice the altitude.

The last two hours are a slow, steady walk into the bowl. Then the ground flattens, the mountains stand up all the way round you, and you are there. Get to bed early. Sunrise is the reason you came.

BLD Sleep: Annapurna Base Camp, teahouse, twin share

Days 4 to 7 · Base camp down to Bamboo, Jhinu Danda, Ghandruk and back to Pokhara 4 to 7 hours a day · 47 km · -2,350 m overall · Ends in Pokhara

Sunrise on Machhapuchhre, then you turn round and walk out. The way down goes faster than the way up and it is harder on your knees, which is what the trekking poles are for. Day 5 gives you the Chhomrong steps in reverse.

Day 6 finishes at the Jhinu Danda hot springs, which are included, and after five days of cold solar showers they land harder than they sound. Day 7 walks out through Ghandruk, a Gurung village with Annapurna South directly behind it, and the jeep brings you back to Lakeside by mid-afternoon.

BLD Sleep: Bamboo, Jhinu Danda and Ghandruk, teahouse, twin share

Days 4, 5, 6 and 7 are grouped here so this sample stays readable. On the built page every day is its own panel.

On the trail

What the walking is actually like

The trail underfoot

Almost none of this route is a path in the flat sense. It is stone: laid steps, worn river rock and, between Chhomrong and Sinuwa, roughly 3,300 cut stone stairs that go down for forty minutes and then straight back up the other side of the valley. Trekking poles matter more here than boots do.

Above Bamboo the stone gives way to a forest floor of roots and mud that stays wet even in October, because the gorge holds cloud until mid morning. The last two hours into the sanctuary are moraine, loose and grey, and that is the only stretch where you will want to watch your feet rather than the view.

A day, start to finish

  • 6:00 Tea in the room. The kitchen is already lit.
  • 7:00 Breakfast, then walking by half past.
  • 11:30 Lunch at a teahouse on the route, cooked to order, so it takes about an hour.
  • 15:00 Into the night stop with the afternoon still open. We finish early on purpose. Cloud comes up the valley around two and the views close.
  • 19:00 Dinner together at one table, usually round the stove.

Charging, water and signal. Every teahouse to Deurali sells power by the hour, about NPR 200 to 300, and solar can fail after a cloudy day, so carry a power bank. Boiled or filtered water is NPR 100 to 200 a litre going up. Ncell holds to Chhomrong and drops out after it.

There is no ATM past Pokhara. Bring cash for the whole week.

The steps below Chhomrong beat me on the way up and beat me again coming down. Everything else on the route is easier than that one hill.

Sample pull quote. Replace or leave out.

The nights

Teahouse rooms are plywood, twin share, with a foam mattress and a blanket that is never quite enough above 3,000 m. Take a liner and a warm layer to sleep in. At Machhapuchhre and Annapurna Base Camp the water in your bottle can freeze overnight in December, so it goes into the bottom of your sleeping bag with you.

Rooms are not booked ahead in high season on this route because lodges will not hold them. We walk early to arrive early, which is how the beds get won.

Sample copy, written for Annapurna Base Camp. Every trip fills this block with its own.

The shape of the week

Route and altitude

You start at 1,780 m and finish the climb at 4,130 m. The whole gain is 2,350 m, spread over three days of climbing. The biggest single day is day 3 at +950 m. You sleep above 3,000 m on two nights only, which is why this trek has a lower rate of altitude sickness than Everest Base Camp, where you sleep above 4,000 m for six.

Difficulty

How hard is it, honestly

Moderate. 4 on our 7 point scale.
Read our full guide to trek grades →

What that means in hours

4 to 7 hours of walking a day for six days, with one day of 8. Not flat. Nepali trails go up and down all day, so a "5 hour day" involves far more climbing than a 5 hour walk at home.

The hardest part

The 3,300 stone steps below Chhomrong on day one, then the same steps in reverse on day five. About two and a half hours of continuous climbing each time. Everyone finds it hard. Nobody has failed to finish it. There is no way around it and no vehicle to take.

The altitude

You sleep above 3,000 m on two nights. That is low compared with Everest Base Camp, where you sleep above 4,000 m for six. Most people get a headache at Machhapuchhre Base Camp and it goes with water, rest and walking slowly. Your guide carries a pulse oximeter and checks you every evening from 2,900 m up.

Who should not book this

If you cannot walk four hours on a hilly path at home without needing a rest day afterwards, book Ghorepani Poon Hill first, 4 days, and come back for this next year. We will say the same thing on the phone. We would rather move you than watch you turn back on day three.

How to train

Three months of one long walk a week, building to 5 hours with a 5 kg pack, plus stairs. Stairs matter more than distance on this route. Read our fitness guide →

When to come

When to walk this one

Four seasons, and the honest version of each. Our view is written into the answer rather than scored in a column.

SeasonWhat it is like, and what we would tell you
SpringMarch to May Rhododendron comes into flower low down through March and peaks in April, which is the best month of the year for it. Mornings are clear, nights above 3,000 m are still cold, and by May the air turns warm and hazy with cloud most afternoons. A good season, and April is one of the two best months to walk this route. April fills up, so book about 8 weeks ahead.
Summer and monsoonJune to August Rain most days, leeches below 2,500 m, landslides on the jeep road to Jhinu Danda, and the mountains hidden behind cloud for days at a time. This is the one season we would rather you did not come. If these are the only months you can travel, ask us about Upper Mustang instead, which sits in the rain shadow and stays dry when everything else is wet.
AutumnSeptember to November September clears after the rain and is green, quiet and underrated, with the odd wet day still. October has the clearest skies of the year and is also the busiest, so lodges fill and your own room is not guaranteed. November is clear and cold with far fewer people. The best season, and if you are choosing between October and November, take November. Same sky, fewer people, better chance of your own room. Book October about 10 weeks ahead.
WinterDecember to February Very cold above Deurali, snow possible at base camp, and some lodges shut for the season. The skies can be superb and the trail is close to empty. Possible with the right kit and the right expectations, but talk to us first so we can tell you what the lodges are doing on your dates.

Safety

If something goes wrong up there

  • Your guide is first aid trained and re-certified every two years
  • She carries a first aid kit, a pulse oximeter and two bottles of emergency oxygen from Chhomrong up
  • From 2,900 m she checks your oxygen saturation and pulse every evening and writes it down
  • If your saturation drops below 85%, or symptoms do not clear overnight, you go down. That decision is your guide's and it is not negotiable
  • Going down 500 m fixes almost everything. There is a lodge roughly every two hours on this route
  • Helicopter evacuation is available from Machhapuchhre Base Camp and Deurali in daylight and clear weather. It is called by our office, not by you. Your insurer is contacted at the same time
  • Our office holds your passport details, insurance policy number and next of kin from the day you book
  • There is mobile signal at Chhomrong, Deurali and Machhapuchhre Base Camp on Ncell, and it is patchy elsewhere. Your guide carries a local SIM

In an emergency, from anywhere: +977 9846845823 Answered 24 hours by Pushpa or Hira.

Kit

What to bring

10 kg maximum for your porter to carry, plus what you carry yourself. Everything else stays in our office in Lakeside, free.

We provide, included in the price

Sleeping bag rated to -10°C, down jacket, duffel bag, trekking poles, water purification tablets. All returned to us in Pokhara.

Footwear

Broken-in boots with ankle support, camp shoes or sandals for the evening, three or four pairs of wool or synthetic socks, and a pair of gaiters if you are walking in December to February.

Clothing layers

Two base layers, one fleece or mid layer, a waterproof shell, two pairs of trekking trousers, and what you sleep in. The down jacket is ours, so leave yours at home.

Head and hands

Sun hat, warm hat, buff, sunglasses rated for altitude, liner gloves and a warmer pair over the top. Hands and ears suffer at base camp more than anything else.

Toiletries and medical

Toilet paper, hand sanitiser, high factor sun cream, lip balm with sun protection, personal medication, blister plasters, and any period supplies you need for the week. See the teahouse section above.

Documents and money

Passport, two passport photographs, insurance policy number, and NPR 12,000 to 18,000 in cash. There is no ATM after Pokhara.

Everything else can be bought or hired in Lakeside, 10 minutes from our office, usually cheaper than at home. Do not buy new boots for this trek. Bring boots you have already walked 50 km in.

Questions

Questions about this trek

Before you book

How fit do I need to be for the Annapurna Base Camp trek?

You need to be able to walk 4 to 7 hours on a hilly path, six days running. If you can walk four hours at home on a Saturday and get up on Sunday without needing a rest day, you are fit enough. Three months of one long walk a week plus stairs will get most people there. Stairs matter more than distance on this route.

Can I do this trek if I have never been to altitude?

Yes, and most of the people who walk it with us have not. You only sleep above 3,000 m on two nights, and the highest of those is 4,130 m. Your guide checks your oxygen saturation every evening from 2,900 m up. Most people get a headache at Machhapuchhre Base Camp and it clears with water, rest and walking slowly.

What is the difference between this and the Ghorepani Poon Hill trek?

Poon Hill is 4 days, tops out at 3,210 m and is a viewpoint trek. This one is 7 days, tops out at 4,130 m and takes you inside the mountains rather than looking at them from a hill. If you are not sure you can do six days of walking, book Poon Hill first.

Can I do it in 5 days instead of 7?

Yes, and we sell it. It is harder rather than easier, because the same climbing gets packed into fewer days and you gain altitude faster. We grade the 5 day version 5 of 7 rather than 4. See the comparison table below.

Do I need a permit, and do you arrange it?

You need an Annapurna Conservation Area Permit. It is included in the price and we arrange it. Bring your passport and two passport photographs.

Travelling as a woman

Can I have a female guide?

Yes, and it is the default rather than a request. Every guide we send on this trek is a licensed woman from this region.

Is there a women-only departure on my dates?

Three of the five fixed departures above are women only, and they cost the same as the mixed ones. If none of them fits your dates, tell us and we will run one privately.

What are the toilets like, and what do I do about my period?

Squat toilets from Deurali up, often in an outside block, and they can freeze above 3,200 m. Nothing on the trail sells pads or tampons, so bring what you need from Pokhara and bring more than you think. Bring sealable bags, because there are no bins above Chhomrong. The teahouse section above covers all of this properly.

Will I have my own room?

On any night the lodge has space, yes, at no extra charge. That is most nights outside October. The exception is the base camp lodge, which fills up. You are never put in a room with a stranger without being asked first.

Money

What is not included in the USD 475?

Travel insurance, hot showers, charging, wifi, drinks other than the one hot drink with each meal, tips, your Nepal visa, and anything caused by weather or illness. Every one of those is priced in the included and not included section above. Budget about USD 575 to 640 all in.

How much cash should I bring on the trail?

NPR 12,000 to 18,000 for the week. There is no ATM after Pokhara, so draw it in Lakeside before you leave.

How do I pay from abroad, and is it safe?

A 20 per cent deposit by bank transfer with no fee from us, or by card through Stripe which adds 4 per cent. You pay the balance in our office in Pokhara. We never ask for the full amount before you arrive, and you should question any Nepali company that does.

On the trail

What happens if I get altitude sickness?

You go down, and going down 500 m fixes almost everything. Your guide checks your oxygen saturation every evening from 2,900 m. If it drops below 85%, or symptoms do not clear overnight, the decision to descend is hers and it is not negotiable. There is a lodge roughly every two hours on this route.

What if the weather closes in and we cannot get to base camp?

Your guide will make the call, usually at Deurali or Machhapuchhre Base Camp. If we cannot get you to base camp safely we do not try. We will use the spare time lower down rather than push, and nobody is charged extra for a day the mountain took away.
